title: NRI Dollar Inflows Surge Past $37 Billion, Driving Decade-High Bank Deposit Growth
excerpt: RBI's special FCNR deposit window has attracted $40.8 billion in total forex inflows since June, already exceeding the $26 billion mobilized in a similar 2013 scheme.
body:
• Indian bank deposits grew 15.4% year-on-year at the end of July, the fastest pace in nearly 10 years, driven by a flood of NRI dollar inflows under the RBI's special FCNR deposit scheme.
  • Non-resident Indians have poured $36.7 billion into FCNR deposits since the scheme launched on June 8, with total forex inflows through the RBI's swap window reaching $40.8 billion by July 31.
  • The inflows have already surpassed the $26 billion mobilized under a similar 2013 scheme, with banks offering NRIs leverage ratios of 9-19x and interest rates of 6-7.5%, with potential returns of up to 14%.
  • The scheme runs until September 30, 2026, and analysts expect total inflows could reach $50-70 billion before the window closes.

Indian bank deposits surged at their fastest pace in nearly a decade at the end of July, propelled by billions of dollars flowing in from overseas Indians through a special Reserve Bank of India deposit scheme designed to shore up the rupee.

Deposits mobilized by scheduled commercial banks rose 15.4% year-on-year, the fastest growth rate since December 2016, when demonetization briefly pushed deposit growth to 15.9%, according to RBI data. Outstanding deposits stood at Rs 269.4 lakh crore at the end of July, up from Rs 233.5 lakh crore a year earlier.

FCNR Scheme Draws Record Inflows

The surge has been powered by the RBI's foreign currency non-resident bank (FCNR-B) deposit window, which was announced on June 5 and rolled out three days later. Under the scheme, the central bank absorbs the full hedging cost for banks raising fresh three-to-five-year FCNR deposits, effectively allowing lenders to offer NRIs substantially higher returns than standard dollar deposits.

Through July 31, the RBI's swap facility received a total of $40.8 billion in forex inflows, with FCNR-B deposits accounting for $36.7 billion — the lion's share. The remaining inflows came through overseas foreign currency borrowings ($2.6 billion) and external commercial borrowings ($1.5 billion).

"The FCNR(B) window will remain open until 30 September, leaving room for more inflows. We believe use of the leveraged borrowing facility by the banks is driving the bulk of the deposit accretion."

— Tanvee Gupta Jain, Chief India Economist, UBS

The scale of the inflows has already eclipsed the $26 billion India mobilized under a similar FCNR scheme in 2013, which was credited with stabilizing the rupee during that year's currency crisis.

Leverage and Returns Fueling NRI Interest

Banks have moved aggressively to attract NRI deposits, offering interest rates of 6-7.5% on FCNR dollar deposits — well above the 5.77% weighted average rate on fresh rupee deposits as of April. State Bank of India raised its FCNR dollar deposit rates by 230-265 basis points to 5.25-6%, while HDFC Bank increased rates to 6% from 3.4-3.65% for three-to-five-year tenures.

The real draw, however, is leverage. Banks and their overseas branches are offering NRIs the ability to borrow against their deposits at ratios of 9-19 times, amplifying effective returns. With the RBI absorbing hedging costs, some structures offer potential returns of up to 14%.

Interest earned on FCNR deposits is also completely tax-free for eligible NRIs, adding to the appeal. The deposits carry a mandatory one-year lock-in period with no premature exit for the first year under the scheme.

Analysts See Room for More

Emkay Global Financial Services projected that flows under the scheme could reach at least $50-55 billion, or 1.2% of GDP, matching levels seen in 2013 and potentially going higher. Axis Bank Executive Director Neeraj Gambhir echoed the optimism.

"In the last round which happened in 2013, most of the money came through the leveraged deposit structures. We expect the same to happen this time as well. The effective returns for the NRI depositors are going to be very good."

— Neeraj Gambhir, Executive Director, Axis Bank

Public sector banks have been more transparent about their targets. Union Bank of India is aiming to garner $1.5-2 billion in FCNR deposits by September, having raised $106 million without leverage so far. Private sector giants including HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, and Axis Bank have been tighter-lipped on specific figures but have confirmed strong NRI response.

Credit Growth Also Accelerates

On the lending side, bank credit growth also picked up, rising 19.4% year-on-year — the fastest pace since June 2024. Outstanding credit stood at Rs 220.8 lakh crore, up from Rs 185 lakh crore a year ago.

The acceleration was driven by renewed corporate demand as higher bond yields pushed companies toward bank borrowing, along with expanded lending to micro, small and medium enterprises through government-backed financial assistance programs introduced in response to the West Asia crisis.

What It Means for NRIs

For diaspora Indians weighing their options, the FCNR window represents a rare convergence of favorable terms — high rates, RBI-backed hedging, tax-free returns, and leverage opportunities — that is unlikely to be replicated once the scheme closes on September 30. The narrowing spread between Indian and U.S. rates compared to 2013, however, means leveraged returns carry more risk if borrowing costs rise.

The scheme's success underscores the financial clout of the Indian diaspora and the RBI's confidence in using NRI capital flows as a tool for currency stabilization — a playbook first tested in 2013 that is now operating at significantly larger scale.
nri_angle: NRIs have poured $37 billion into Indian bank FCNR deposits through a special RBI scheme offering tax-free, leveraged returns of up to 14%, with the window closing September 30.
